wbs.instructions: Drag each word into its blank — or tap a word, then tap a blank.
text: A ___ breaks a project into ___ with ___ and ___ .
wbs.explanation: A WBS decomposes work into tasks, annotated with dependencies and milestones. Gantt charts and poker come later — they consume the WBS, they are not part of it.
hints: The acronym names the whole structure.

wbs.prompt: Put the planning workflow in order
wbs.instructions: Drag rows into sequence — one continuous drag does it. Alt+↑/↓ works from the keyboard.

items.label: Break the project into WBS tasks
Record dependencies in a task table
Compute ES/EF, LS/LF, slack, critical path

wbs.explanation: Decompose → estimate → order → draw → time-analyse. Every later step eats the earlier step's output, which is why a sloppy WBS poisons the whole plan.

text: Slack = ___ − ___ . The ___ path is the zero-slack chain.
critical-path.explanation: Slack = LS − ES (equivalently LF − EF). The zero-slack chain is the critical path — the longest path, which sets the shortest possible duration.
Forwards for earliest and duration, backwards for latest, subtract for slack, chain the zeros — then verify the chain sums to the duration.

critical-path.prompt: Click the 10-week activity on the critical chain
critical-path.instructions: Select the D task in the Project A network.
critical-path.explanation: D (10 weeks) sits on A → D → F → G → H. It has zero slack: any slip delays the 25-week deadline.

activity-graphs.prompt: In which diagram do the arrows represent activities?

distractor.0: In AON, activities are the nodes (boxes); arrows are only dependencies.
distractor.2: They encode the same project differently — work lives on nodes in one, arrows in the other.
distractor.3: Arrows mean 'must complete before', not data flow.

activity-graphs.explanation: AOA puts work on arrows (nodes are instants, sometimes needing dummy tasks); AON puts work on nodes.

gantt-charts.prompt: On the mini Gantt sketch, which activity could absorb a 2-week delay without moving the deadline?
gantt-charts.explanation: Only slack absorbs delay. B carries 4 weeks of float; every gold (critical) bar would move the deadline immediately.

lifecycle-models.prompt: Match each situation to its fitting model

pairNotes.r: Spiral exists to buy down risk per cycle — that is its whole point.
pairNotes.u: A prototype answers one question fast; it is not a first draft of the product.

lifecycle-models.explanation: Stable → waterfall's cheap sequence; risky → spiral's risk cycles; doubtful → prototype the question before committing.
The lecture's phase order. Iterative waterfall keeps the order but adds feedback loops — a test failure can send work back to design.

estimation-planning-poker.prompt: Planning poker reveals estimates simultaneously to prevent anchoring.
estimation-planning-poker.confirm: Face-down reveal stops juniors anchoring on the first loud number; outliers then explain and the team re-estimates.
estimation-planning-poker.explanation: Simultaneous reveal defeats anchoring. Divergent cards trigger discussion about what the task really involves.
Conceal → reveal → discuss → converge. '?' and ∞ are legitimate bids: clarify or split the task.

scrum-framework.prompt: Match each accountability to its job
scrum-framework.explanation: One owner of priorities, one team building the increment, one guardian of the process — and the team manages itself.

scrum-framework.prompt: The Scrum Master assigns tasks to developers.

distractor.0: The team is self-managing: members decide internally who does what. The Scrum Master guards the process, never the task list.

scrum-framework.explanation: False. Self-managing teams allocate their own work; the Scrum Master removes barriers and protects the process.

scrum-events-backlogs.explanation: Commit, steer, inspect the product with stakeholders, then improve the process. Review looks outward; retrospective looks inward.

scrum-events-backlogs.prompt: Which event inspects the product with stakeholders?

distractor.0: Planning commits to the goal — inspection happens at the end.
distractor.1: Dailies steer the Developers' own plan.
distractor.3: The retrospective inspects the process, within the team only.

scrum-events-backlogs.explanation: The review demos the increment to stakeholders and adapts the backlog; the retrospective follows and improves how the team works.

text: Actual progress = sum of ___ durations of tasks ___ by time t.
burn-up-charts.explanation: Actual progress adds estimated durations of finished tasks — earned value. Using actual durations instead is the classic exam trap.

burn-up-charts.prompt: Burn-up actual progress is computed from how long finished tasks actually took.

distractor.0: It uses their estimated durations — finishing a 20-day-estimate task in 30 days still earns 20.

burn-up-charts.explanation: False. Earned value = estimates of completed work, which is why planned and actual lines are comparable.

burn-up-charts.instructions: Read the SUMIF helper, then predict actual progress at day 30.
burn-up-charts.code:
Planned = SUM(B2:B20)          // 200
Rate    = Planned / Duration   // 200 / 100
Actual  = SUMIF(Finish, "<=" & T, B)
// tasks finished by day 30: estimates 20, 10, 15
burn-up-charts.explanation: SUMIF adds estimates only for finished tasks: 20 + 10 + 15 = 45. Planned at day 30 is 60 — so the project trails.
hints: SUMIF filters by the finish column first.
Add the three estimates, not the day.

kanban-wip.prompt: Scenario: a 'Done' card turns out defective
kanban-wip.instructions: You are on a team with a WIP limit of 3. 'Search Courses' is Done — but a user reports it crashes on empty queries. Decide what happens next.

alert.text: Bug report lands: 'Search Courses' (in Done) crashes on empty queries. Review is full (3/3), Coding has 1 card. What do you do first?

options.label: Pull fresh work into Coding anyway
options.note: Starting new work while a defect escapes violates finish-before-start.

options.label: Move the card back to Coding/Testing and fix it within WIP
options.note: Done means accepted — a defective card re-enters the flow.

options.label: Ask to raise the WIP limit so everything fits
options.note: Raising WIP hides the constraint instead of resolving it.

rushed.text: Two streams now compete: the defect and the new feature. Review stays clogged; the crash reaches more users.
rushed.title: Split focus
rushed.debrief: WIP limits exist to force finishing over starting. New work while a known defect escapes multiplies rework.

limit.text: The board absorbs everything — columns swell to 5, 6, 7 cards. Nothing finishes; the pile-up signal is gone.
limit.title: Limit inflated
limit.debrief: A WIP limit you raise whenever it binds is decoration. The pile-up was the diagnosis; the fix was rebalancing toward Review.

fixing.text: The card is back in Coding/Testing and the crash is fixed. Review still holds 3 cards. How does the fix reach Done?

options.label: Merge it straight to Done — it was Done before
options.note: Fixes re-break things; the lecture says regressions re-occur.

options.label: Let it flow through Review and Awaiting Merge again

sloppy.text: The fix ships unreviewed and breaks saved searches. Another card travels backwards — the team now distrusts Done.
sloppy.title: Unreviewed merge
sloppy.debrief: Regression discipline is the point of the Review column. Every fix gets re-reviewed, or Done stops meaning accepted.

solid.text: Re-reviewed, re-merged, re-accepted. The board kept flowing because the team finished the defect before starting anything new.
solid.title: Discipline held
solid.debrief: Move Done defects back, respect WIP, re-review fixes. That is the whole Kanban contract in one incident.

kanban-wip.explanation: Kanban incidents test one habit: finish before you start. The board's columns and WIP limit tell you exactly where defective work belongs.

code-review.prompt: Find the bug in the progress helper
code-review.instructions: Click the faulty line. Context: Worksheet 2's SUMIF crash-course.
code-review.code:
// planned vs actual helper
Planned = SUM(B2:B20)
Actual = SUMIF(A2:A20, H1, B2:B20)
Status = IF(Actual >= Planned, "ahead", "behind")
code-review.explanation: Line 3 passes H1 as a literal match instead of a comparison: it needs ">=" & H1 (or "<=" & T for finished-by-time). Without the operator string, only exact matches count.
hints: SUMIF's second parameter is a condition string.
How do you say 'greater than or equal to H1' in a formula?

code-review.prompt: A good checklist lets reviewers stop thinking about the code.

distractor.0: The slides say checklists help juniors and get in the way for experts — judgement stays with the human.

code-review.explanation: False. Automate what checks can be automated; spend human attention on logic. Checklists guide, never replace, judgement.

exam-mistakes-agile.prompt: Ahead on the burn-up while scope keeps growing means the project is safe.

distractor.0: Rising scope with flat actuals is the classic distress signal — the gap that matters includes the scope line.

exam-mistakes-agile.explanation: False. Read all three lines: actual vs planned vs scope. Growth can swallow any lead.
